title: Smeared-slot scheduler: simulator notes & ops checklist
body:
Purpose and rough summary:

This is a working note describing the "smeared-slot" scheduling idea, the simulator we should build to evaluate it, and an ops checklist for spinning up a prototype in the lab. The core idea: instead of fixed token-window coalescing or pure request-level batching we 'smear' token service opportunities probabilistically across lightweight slots so that short and long requests both make forward progress and KV cache warmup costs remain bounded. The smear is a tunable distribution that spreads tokens from oversized requests across upcoming slots to reduce tail interference for short, latency-sensitive requests while preserving kernel-friendly batch sizes.

Why try this (motivation):
- Observed issue: long-token requests (LLR) dominate slots, causing short requests to queue and suffer P95+/tail latency inflation.
- Pure token-level fairness (strict per-token round robin) yields excessive kernel churn and harms batching affinity (small kernels per slot).
- Pure request-level fairness (serve whole request when scheduled) causes starvation and poor fairness for high-arrival-rate short requests.
- Need middle ground that: (a) protects short request latency, (b) maintains decent average batch sizes for kernel throughput, (c) controls KV cache churn/cold misses.

Design sketch (behavioral):
- Time is divided into scheduling ticks (slots). Each slot can trigger an inference kernel with a target token budget T_slot (configurable).
- Incoming requests are classified into types: Short (S, <= 64 tokens), Medium (M, 65-512), Long (L, >512). We keep queue per client or per request-class depending on policy.
- For each long request, rather than enqueuing the entire token tail, we maintain a pending-token counter and place it into a smear queue with a probabilistic release schedule.
- Smearing distribution: geometric or truncated Poisson with mean mu; each slot we sample how many tokens to release from each smeared long request up to T_slot remaining capacity. This spreads service over N slots so that any single slot isn't overwhelmed.
- Admission priority: Short requests get strict low-latency lanes (token budget reserve), medium requests share a middle lane, smeared long requests fill leftover capacity but cannot evict reserved capacity.

KV cache & kernel affinity considerations:
- We add a warmup bias: prefer to complete at least R_warmup tokens from a given model stream before switching to another model/sequence to reduce KV thrash. This bias interacts with smear by ensuring any smear release contains a minimum contiguous prefix length (min_chunk), otherwise skip and postpone release to next slot.
- Kernel affinity score = alpha * contiguous_prefix + beta * batch_size + gamma * model_switch_penalty. Scheduler tries to maximize score under latency constraints. alpha/beta/gamma are tunables exposed to tuning framework.

Fairness objectives (what we measure):
- Latency fairness: per-client P50/P95/P99 for short-requests vs baseline; fairness measured with Jain's index over per-client mean latency.
- Token fairness: fraction of tokens served per client normalized by traffic demand; compute Jain's on tokens/sec per client over a window.
- Starvation windows: max time any request waits before first token served.
- Throughput cost: effective tokens/sec and kernel utilization.
- KV miss rate: fraction of requests that experience cold KV miss on first generation after model or sequence context switch.

Simulator design (event-driven):
- Inputs: real trace snippets (chatty short-request heavy, mixed enterprise long-completion heavy), synthetic bursty and steady-state profiles, model catalog (seq-len distribution, kv-warmup cost, kernel latency curve as function of batch size and prefix length).
- State: queue per priority lane; smeared-token ledger per long-request; current slot clock; KV cache state (per-model per-worker recent-key set, TTL).
- Events: arrival, slot-trigger, kernel-complete, kv-evict, sample-release.
- Outputs: time-series of latencies, slot batch sizes, kernel runtimes, KV misses.

Pseudocode (high level):
- On arrival(request r):
    if r.len <= short_threshold: enqueue(short_lane, r)
    else if r.len <= medium_threshold: enqueue(medium_lane, r)
    else: create smeared_ledger[r.id] = r.len; enqueue(smear_pool, r.id)

- On slot_tick():
    allocate reserved capacity R_short, R_med; remaining_capacity = T_slot - R_short - R_med
    form batch = drain(short_lane, R_short) + drain(medium_lane, R_med)
    for each smeared_id in smear_pool in round-robin:
        x = sample_smear(smeared_id, remaining_capacity)
        if x >= min_chunk and remaining_capacity >= x:
            attach x tokens from smeared_id to batch
            smeared_ledger[smeared_id] -= x
            remaining_capacity -= x
        if smeared_ledger[smeared_id] == 0: remove from smear_pool
    if kernel_affinity_score(batch) below threshold and remaining_capacity > 0: try to merge adjacent small batches (prefetch from next slot)
    submit_kernel(batch)

Key knobs to sweep in simulation:
- T_slot (token capacity per slot): 64/128/256/512
- smear mean (mu) and distribution (geometric vs truncated-normal)
- min_chunk (minimum contiguous tokens when releasing from smear)
- R_short reserve fraction (0-30%)
- KV warmup bias (R_warmup contiguous tokens preferred)
- affinity weights alpha/beta/gamma

Experiment matrix (initial):
- Traces: short-heavy_2023-chat, mixed-enterprise-v2, long-burst
- Sweep T_slot x smear_mu x R_short x min_chunk
- Baselines: pure request-level FIFO, token-RR, existing continuous-batcher (current mainline)
- Metrics: P50/P95/P99 latency short & medium, Jain(token fairness), average kernel throughput, KV miss rate, overall cost estimate (tokens/second * kernel-ms cost function)

Operational considerations for prototype (ops checklist):
- Simulator infra:
  - Dockerized simulator with config yaml for trace & model profiles
  - Log outputs: per-slot CSV (timestamp,batch_size,kernel_ms,kv_misses), per-request csv (arrival,first_token_ts,completion_ts)
  - Visualization: quick Grafana dashboard from CSVs or use Jupyter notebooks
- Lab deployment for A/B:
  - Implement smeared-slot scheduler as a pluggable strategy behind the runtime scheduler interface (flag: SCHED_STRATEGY=smeared_slot)
  - Add feature flag gating + Canary route in console for internal test org
  - Canary pods set to low capacity and synthetic traffic generator to replay traces
  - Instrumentation: add per-request telemetry for "tokens_released_by_smear" and "kv_warmup_hits"
- Safety knobs:
  - global throughput cap to avoid oversubmitting kernels during misconfiguration
  - watchdog that disables smear if observed P99 short-request exceeds threshold

Open questions and risks:
- Does smear add unacceptable head-of-line splitting complexity to response reassembly (ordering/streaming)? Need to prototype streaming handler that stitches partial outputs in-order with minimal jitter.
- Interaction with function/tool-calls and multi-turn chat where context must be contiguous: smear may harm coherence. Consider per-conversation affinity exemption or require min_chunk equal to conversational boundary.
- Multi-model workload: smear across different model families may cause KV thrash; require smear pool partitioned by model family and per-worker affinity enforcement.
- Fairness across tenants where tenants have very different request length distributions: need per-tenant smear policies or budgeted token quotas. Explore credit-based smear where long-tenants accrue smear debt.

Next steps / short-term plan:
- Week 0-1: implement small event-driven simulator, validate with short-heavy and mixed traces. Target: reproducible CSVs. (Owners: Priya, Ethan)
- Week 1-2: run sweep for T_slot x smear_mu x R_short, produce comparison plots vs baseline. (Owners: Sofia)
- Week 2-3: prototype in runtime as feature-flagged scheduler; route limited internal traffic and run canary. (Owners: Liam)
- Week 3: gather metrics, decide whether smear provides a Pareto improvement (tail latency down, kernel throughput comparable).

Notes to self / heuristics learned while sketching:
- Keep smear mean small relative to expected request lengths; too large smear ~ request-level behavior, too small smear ~ token RR.
- min_chunk helps maintain kernel affinity; tune against kernel latency curves.
- Reserve a small fraction for extremely short requests; this avoids worst-case tail behavior with minimal throughput loss.

Appendix: useful traces / primitives to add to corpus:
- reply-heavy-concise-chat-2023-12 (lots of 8-20 token responses),
- enterprise-qa-longform (1-2k tokens monthly batch jobs),
- bursty-bot-surge (bursts of short requests at 10k rps for 1s every 30s).

TODO (short):
- [ ] Create minimal trace DSL and loader for simulator
- [ ] Implement KV cache model (cost per context-switch)
- [ ] Hook in kernel cost curves from bench harness
- [ ] Draft canary run playbook and Slack alert thresholds

If this approach looks promising after simulation we should write a compact design doc (2-pager) for product/console folks showing tradeoffs and config knobs they can expose in the Console. For now this is a lightweight working doc — please add comments or drop JIRA links to specific tickets you want me to pull into the experiment plan.
